newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open unchanged, no economic data due.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open unchanged, no economic data due.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened unchanged on Wednesday, in line with overseas trends.
The dollar's overnight climb to a new 56-month high of 126.90 against the yen lent scant support to Treasuries, analysts said.
The dollar traded at a 56-month high against the yen in London on Wednesday and climbed against the mark.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond opened unchanged in New York at 94-4/32, yielding 7.10 percent. Two-year notes also opened unchanged at 99-22/32, yielding 6.42 percent.

"It's going to be a quiet day today because there's no real data," said Astrid Adolfson, vice president and financial economist at MCM Moneywatch. "There was a little buying overnight, but very light."

Adolfson said most participants want to stay sidelined until they see Friday's March wholesale price and retail sales data. Adolfson said there's "probably more concern" in the market about the strength of retail sales in March than there has to be. A Reuters poll forecast that retail sales rose 0.6 percent in March after a 0.8 percent February rise.
But Adolfson said the bond market recognizes that "the economy is still roaring ahead.
"Companies are reporting good earnings and sales and the Federal Reserves seems set on raising rates," she said.
While Treasuries opened unchanged despite new strength in the dollar, the U.S. unit could still be a positive factor for bond prices, analysts said.
"The dollar is keeping a floor under Treasury prices right now," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.

Given the absence of any economic reports on Wednesday, the strong dollar could propel Treasuries prices "somewhat higher," Flanagan said. But he said other factors would keep a cap on Treasury market gains.

"You're limited as to how far you can go because some fundamental problems (for the credit markets) still exist," Flanagan said. "We have an economy that is growing strongly. Demand continues to exceed expectations and inventories are not accumulating at all. Regarding wage pressures, Flanagan said, "we're beginning to see the upward trajectory kick in more and more with each new employment report."

Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Gary Stern is scheduled to speak at Moorhead State University's Business and Industry Day at 1300/1700. The market will listen to his remarks but Stern spoke in Duluth, Minn. on Tuesday and his talk is not expected to have a market impact.
"(The Fed presidents) usually give pretty much the same speech so there's usually nothing new," said Adolfson.
"Everyone knows that Stern tends to take a more hawkish tone anyway so I'd tend to think (his speech won't have an impact)," said Flanagan.
Five-year notes opened near unchanged but climbed 3/32 to 99-18/32 in early trade to yield 6.73 percent. Ten-year notes also headed higher, rising 4/32 to 95-19/32, yielding 6.87 percent.
Three-year bill rates were unchanged at 5.10 percent. Six-month and year-bill rates eased one basis point each to 5.33 percent and 5.62 percent, respectively.
